title: AI phone answering for burger restaurant orders
description: An AI phone host can take burger takeout orders, answer menu questions, forward calls, and keep the counter moving during busy hours.
question: How can I handle burger restaurant phone orders without missing calls or tying up staff?
answer: An AI phone host can answer your burger joint’s phone, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, answer common questions, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. With ROAL, you can set it up from your website or menu, forward calls from your existing number, and pay only for completed orders that reach the kitchen screen.
summary: Learn how to set up phone orders for a burger joint, what the host can handle, and how to route tricky calls to staff.
intro:
Burger restaurant phone orders are usually simple, but they pile up fast during lunch, dinner, and late-night rushes. An AI phone host like ROAL can answer those calls, take the order, and send it to the kitchen while your team keeps cooking.

For a busy burger joint, that means fewer interruptions and cleaner tickets. It also gives callers a fast way to ask about hours, parking, toppings, sides, and sold-out items without waiting on hold.

sections.h2: What should an AI phone host handle at a burger joint?
sections.body:
A good phone host for a burger spot should handle the calls that come in all day long: pickup orders, delivery orders, hours, address, parking, and menu questions. ROAL does that from your live menu, so if you mark an item sold out, it won’t offer it on the call.

For burger restaurant phone orders, the important part is accuracy. The host should collect the item, size, modifiers, and notes, then repeat the order back before sending it to the kitchen. It should also collect the caller’s name and phone number and quote a ready time.

A simple burger call flow looks like this:
1. Caller asks for pickup.
2. Host confirms the menu item and toppings.
3. Host checks for sauces, sides, and drink choices.
4. Host repeats the order and ready time.
5. Host sends the ticket to the kitchen screen.

Example script line: “What would you like on the burger, and would you like fries or onion rings with that?”

If a caller asks something tricky, like a complaint, a catering request, or a serious allergy question, ROAL hands it to staff with a summary. That keeps the main order flow moving while still protecting the customer experience.

sections.h2: How do burger restaurant phone orders get taken cleanly?
sections.body:
The cleanest setup is to treat the phone like another order channel, not a side task. Your phone host should read from the same menu your kitchen uses, so the order on the call matches the ticket at prep.

Here is a practical checklist for burger restaurant phone orders:
- Keep burger names short and consistent.
- Make toppings and add-ons easy to hear.
- List common sides clearly.
- Mark sold-out items in the menu editor.
- Decide how you want to phrase doneness, if you use it.
- Set ready times that match your kitchen pace.

Worked example: say your average burger order is $28. A customer orders two burgers, fries, and drinks for pickup. The host takes the order, confirms it, and sends it to the kitchen screen. If you want to plug in your own numbers, replace that $28 with your average ticket and track how many calls turn into completed orders.

ROAL also keeps call history with transcripts and recordings, so you can review where callers get confused. If customers keep asking the same thing, add it to FAQs once and the host will know it from then on. That is useful for busy burger spots with the same few questions all day long.

sections.h2: How much does it cost compared with other order channels?
sections.body:
For many burger joints, phone orders cost less than delivery apps and are easier to control than a full-time phone hire. Third-party delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order, which can add up fast on burger tickets with sides and drinks.

ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reached the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free, and billing is monthly.

| Channel | Typical cost style | What to plug in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery apps | Roughly 15-30% commission | Your average order value |
| Human answering service | Per minute or per call | Your call volume |
| Monthly AI phone tools | Fixed monthly fee | Whether orders come in or not |

Example: if you get 100 completed phone orders in a month, that would be 100 x $0.90, or $90. Replace that with your own order count. sections.h2: How do I set it up without changing my phone number?
sections.body:
You can keep your restaurant’s existing number. The setup flow is simple: paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, and ROAL reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or menu uploads.

Then you test-call the phone host right in the browser. No sign-up is needed for that test. When you’re ready to go live, you claim the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your existing number to it. You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered.

A practical setup checklist:
- Check that the burger menu is current.
- Make sure hours and address are correct.
- Decide which calls should forward only when busy.
- Choose the host’s voice and name.
- Test a few burger orders before turning it on.

If you want a quick place to start, ROAL’s [How it works](/how-it-works) page explains the flow, and [Call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) can help you find the right forwarding steps. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.

sections.h2: What happens when the call is not a simple burger order?
sections.body:
Not every call should stay in the phone host. Some calls need a person, especially when the caller has a complaint, a catering request, a serious allergy-sensitive question, or wants a manager. ROAL sends those to staff with a summary so your team can step in with context.

That matters for burger joints because the phone gets a lot of mixed traffic. A caller may want a cheeseburger pickup order, then ask about parking, then ask if an ingredient is sold out. The phone host should handle the easy part and move the hard part to staff.

Use this simple rule set:
1. Let the host handle standard orders and menu questions.
2. Let staff handle manager requests and complaints.
3. Let staff review allergy-sensitive questions before confirming anything.
4. Keep a short FAQ list for repeat questions.

Example script line for a handoff: “I can connect this to the team now, and I’ll pass along the details so they have your order history.”

ROAL also speaks the caller’s language, which helps when your neighborhood gets a mix of callers. If a question is not covered, it lands in an inbox. You answer once, and the host knows it from then on. That is useful for burger shops that get the same special requests every week.

sections.h2: What should burger shop owners check before going live?
sections.body:
Before you turn on burger restaurant phone orders, take ten minutes to check the details that affect the call. Small mistakes here create repeat work later, especially on busy nights.

Use this launch checklist:
- Menu items match what you actually serve.
- Prices are current.
- Hours are correct for dine-in, pickup, and late-night service.
- Address and parking notes are clear.
- Common modifiers are listed, like cheese, bacon, extra sauce, and no onions.
- Sold-out items are marked correctly.
- The kitchen screen is ready to receive tickets.
- Someone on staff knows where to find the inbox for unanswered questions.

ROAL includes a dashboard with live tickets, call history with transcripts and recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. That helps if you run one burger shop now and add another later.

If you want to compare ROAL with hiring phone staff or a press-1 menu, the [comparison pages](/compare) are a good place to start. For burger owners specifically, you can also read more on [ROAL for burger joints](/for/burgers). A short test run is the best way to spot anything your menu needs before you go live.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take burger restaurant phone orders accurately?
faq.a: Yes, if the menu and hours are set correctly. ROAL takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the restaurant’s live menu, then confirms the order back before sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also avoids offering items marked sold out.

faq.q: How do I forward my burger shop’s phone to ROAL?
faq.a: You keep your existing number and forward calls to the phone line ROAL gives each location. You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered, depending on how you want to run your shop. Always confirm the exact forwarding steps with your carrier and test with a real call.

faq.q: Does ROAL take card payments over the phone?
faq.a: No. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes payment. That keeps the phone order process simple and aligned with your current checkout setup.

faq.q: What kinds of burger calls should go to staff instead of the phone host?
faq.a: Calls about complaints, catering, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests should go to staff. ROAL hands those off with a summary so your team has context. It still handles the standard order and menu questions on its own.
